picks.rationale: Concrete, actionable AI tool release: Amazon expanded Kindle Translate, its free AI translation service for KDP indie authors, from two language pairs to six languages (EN, ES, DE, FR, IT, PT), with in-tool formatting, pricing, publishing and automatic accuracy checks. Directly changes how self-pub authors localize and reach global readers. Distinct outlet and topic from published kindle-recaps and Ailaysa translation AI.
picks.excerpt: Amazon has expanded Kindle Translate, its free AI-powered translation service for KDP indie authors, from two language pairs to six languages - English, Spanish, German, French, Italian and Portuguese. Authors can create, manage, price and publish fully formatted machine-translated editions of their books in a few clicks, with automatic accuracy checks before publication.

picks.rationale: Freshest craft/production hook: two dueling new surveys on AI audiobook narration - a Spoken study found 61% of listeners mistook AI voices for human and favored them in multi-character scenes, while an Audio Publishers Association study shows willingness to try AI narration fell from 70% (2025) to 61% (2026). A concrete new data point (multi-cast AI voices) that changes how audiobook producers weigh AI narration; distinct survey/angle from the published anu-audiobook report and cartland-clone story.
picks.excerpt: Two dueling surveys on AI audiobook narration: a Spoken-commissioned study found 61% of listeners mistook AI voices for human and favored them in multi-character scenes, while an Audio Publishers Association study shows willingness to try AI narration fell from 70% (2025) to 61% (2026) - human narration still preferred.

picks.rationale: The single AI-legal pick kept (override #4): a new class-action by Cengage, Elsevier and Hachette accusing Google of copying millions of books to train Gemini - a distinct lawsuit from the earlier PLS litigation already published. picks.excerpt: Publishers including Cengage, Elsevier and Hachette have filed a class-action suit against Google, accusing it of illegally copying millions of books to train its Gemini AI service - the latest front in the fight over whether published books can be used as AI training data.
